sections.section_title: The Minor Heir -- Owner of Everything, Free as a Slave
sections.summary: Paul illustrates the condition of an heir during minority: though owner of everything, the child is no different from a slave, subject to guardians and managers until the date set by the father.

sections.section_title: Enslaved under the Stoicheia -- Redeemed by the Son
sections.summary: Paul describes the pre-Christ condition as enslavement under the elementary things of the world, and declares that when the fullness of time came God sent his Son, born under the law, to redeem those under the law so that all believers could receive adoption as sons.

sections.section_title: The Spirit of the Son -- Evidence of Sonship
sections.summary: Paul declares that because the Galatians are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts crying 'Abba, Father,' so that each believer is no longer a slave but a son and heir through God.

Paul warns the Galatians that their adoption of Torah observance -- observing days, months, seasons, and years -- constitutes a regression from knowing God back into enslavement to weak and worthless elementary things, and expresses fear that his labor among them may have been in vain.
sections.relevance: The passage describes believers who have 'come to know God, or rather to be known by God' (4:9) as being in the active process of turning back to bondage. Paul's self-correction ('or rather to be known by God') places the initiative with God -- God knew them, God chose them -- yet this divine knowing does not prevent their voluntary return to slavery. The fear that his labor was 'in vain' (4:11) implies that the entire process of the Galatians' coming to know God could be rendered fruitless by their regression. The passage presupposes that being known by God does not automatically preserve the known from voluntarily returning to bondage.
key_phrases: now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary things?
Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?
I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain

sections.section_title: The Personal Appeal -- Remember How You Received Me
sections.summary: Paul makes a personal appeal recalling the Galatians' extraordinary initial reception of him despite his bodily ailment, and laments that their former blessedness has been replaced by estrangement now that he has told them the truth.

sections.section_title: The Rival Teachers' Motives and Paul's Anguish
sections.summary: Paul exposes the rival teachers' corrupt motives of creating dependency through exclusion, and expresses his own anguish in the language of childbirth, laboring again until Christ is formed in the Galatians.

sections.section_title: The Two Sons of Abraham -- Flesh and Promise
sections.summary: Paul asks those who want to be under the law whether they have listened to the law, then recounts that Abraham had two sons: one born to a slave woman according to the flesh and one born to a free woman through promise.

Paul reads the Hagar-Sarah narrative allegorically as representing two covenants: Hagar corresponds to the Sinai covenant producing children for slavery and to the present Jerusalem, while the Jerusalem above is free and is the mother of believers, citing Isaiah 54:1 about the barren woman's children outnumbering those of the married woman.

sections.section_title: The Application -- Children of Promise, Not of Flesh
sections.summary: Paul identifies the Galatian believers as children of promise like Isaac, notes the pattern of the flesh-born persecuting the Spirit-born, cites the Torah's command to cast out the slave woman and her son since they cannot share the inheritance with the free woman's son, and concludes that believers are children of the free woman.
